name: Chlamydia
definition: A sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
overview: Chlamydia is a bacterial infection that is usually spread through sex. Many people have no symptoms and do not know they have it. When symptoms do occur they can include unusual discharge, pain when passing urine, and pelvic or testicular pain. It is curable with antibiotics, but untreated infection can cause problems such as pelvic inflammatory disease and can affect fertility. Testing uses a urine sample or a swab.
causes: Infection with the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
It is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex, or contact with infected genital fluids such as semen or vaginal fluid.
Sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used can also pass it on.
An untreated infection can pass from a pregnant person to the baby during birth.
It is not spread by casual contact such as kissing, hugging or sharing towels or toilet seats.
riskFactors: A sexual partner who has a sexually transmitted infection.
Being a sexually active woman under 25, the group the English screening programme prioritises.
signs: Unusual vaginal discharge or discharge from the penis.
Bleeding after sex or between periods.
Pain or swelling in the testicles.
complications: Pelvic inflammatory disease in women, when the infection spreads to the womb, ovaries or fallopian tubes.
Difficulty getting pregnant or infertility, long-lasting pelvic pain and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy after pelvic inflammatory disease.
Pain and swelling of the epididymis in men, which the NHS describes as very rare.
Premature labour and low birthweight when infection is untreated in pregnancy.
Eye infection or pneumonia in a newborn who caught the infection during birth.
diagnosis: Chlamydia is diagnosed by testing a urine sample or a swab. The test most often used is a nucleic acid amplification test, known as a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard. Some services offer online test kits. A sexual health service notes that a very recent infection may not show up on a test straight away. In England the national screening programme recommends that sexually active women under 25 are tested each year and after each new partner.
treatment: Chlamydia is curable with antibiotics. The standard antibiotic options are doxycycline and azithromycin tablets. The 2026 BASHH guideline makes doxycycline the first-line treatment, with azithromycin used only where another infection, Mycoplasma genitalium, has been excluded. Partners are also tested and treated. Sexual activity is paused until treatment and any tests are complete. People diagnosed are offered a repeat test some months after treatment to check for reinfection.
prevention: Correct and consistent use of condoms during sex is the most effective way to prevent chlamydia. The NHS also describes condoms or dental dams for oral sex, and washing sex toys or covering them with a new condom each time. There is no vaccine against chlamydia. The NHS advises testing once a year or when there is a new sexual partner.
seekCare: A sexual health service can arrange testing for people with or without symptoms, for a new sexual partner, or after a partner is diagnosed; the NHS advises testing once a year or with a new partner. Severe pelvic or testicular pain, or feeling very unwell, needs urgent help from NHS 111 or the GP the same day, and a call to 999 in an emergency.

references.title: BASHH: National guideline for the management of infection with Chlamydia trachomatis (2026)

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of chlamydia?
sections.body:
Most people with chlamydia do not notice any symptoms and do not know they have it. When symptoms do occur, they may take weeks to appear after sex with someone who has chlamydia. Because symptoms are often absent, the infection can go unnoticed until a test is done.

In women, symptoms can include unusual vaginal discharge, pain when passing urine, pain in the tummy or pelvis, bleeding after sex and bleeding between periods. Painful sex and rectal pain or discharge have also been listed by the CDC. The CDC adds that chlamydia can damage the reproductive system of a woman even when it causes no symptoms.

In men, symptoms can include discharge from the penis, burning when passing urine, and pain or swelling in the testicles. Infection of the rectum can also cause symptoms in both women and men.

sections.heading: How is chlamydia passed on?
sections.body:
Chlamydia is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis. It is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex, or through contact with infected genital fluids such as semen or vaginal fluid. The NHS describes sex without a condom as a common route of infection. It can also be passed on by sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time they are used.

Casual contact such as kissing, hugging or sharing towels or toilet seats does not spread it. The CDC lists a new sexual partner, more than one partner and a partner with a sexually transmitted infection as situations of increased risk. An untreated infection can also pass from a pregnant person to the baby during birth.

sections.heading: How is chlamydia diagnosed, and who is offered screening?
sections.body:
Chlamydia is diagnosed by testing a urine sample or a swab. The test most often used is a nucleic acid amplification test, known as a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard. Some services offer online test kits. A sexual health service notes that a very recent infection may not show up on a test straight away.

In England the National Chlamydia Screening Programme focuses on sexually active women under 25, who are recommended to test each year and after each new partner. Young men can still get tests at sexual health services, and are contacted and tested through partner notification. More generally, the NHS advises testing once a year or when there is a new sexual partner. Anyone diagnosed is offered a discussion about partner notification, so that recent partners can be tested and treated.

sections.heading: How is chlamydia treated?
sections.body:
Chlamydia is curable with antibiotics. The standard antibiotic options are doxycycline and azithromycin tablets. The 2026 BASHH guideline makes doxycycline the first-line treatment, with azithromycin used only where another infection, Mycoplasma genitalium, has been excluded.

Partners are also tested and treated. Sexual activity is paused until treatment and any tests are complete. WHO advises waiting after finishing the medicine before having sex, or using condoms correctly. Older BASHH guidance says current partners should be treated whatever their own test result. The same guidance advised that the person and treated partners avoid sex, including oral sex and sex with condoms, for a time after treatment.

People diagnosed are offered another test some months after treatment, to look for reinfection. One Scottish guideline says a routine test of cure is not required.

sections.heading: What problems can untreated chlamydia cause?
sections.body:
Untreated chlamydia can cause serious problems, but WHO says long-term problems are unlikely if it is treated early. In women the infection can spread to the womb, ovaries or fallopian tubes and cause pelvic inflammatory disease. This can lead to difficulty getting pregnant, long-lasting pelvic pain and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy. Pelvic inflammatory disease is usually treated with a course of antibiotics.

In men, the infection can spread to the testicles and epididymis, causing pain and swelling, though the NHS describes this as very rare. The NHS says untreated infection might affect fertility in men, while the CDC says men rarely have health problems from chlamydia. In pregnancy, untreated chlamydia may increase the risk of premature labour and low birthweight, and the baby may develop an eye infection or pneumonia after birth.

sections.heading: How can chlamydia be prevented?
sections.body:
WHO says correct and consistent use of condoms during sex is the most effective way to prevent chlamydia. The NHS also describes condoms or dental dams for oral sex, and washing sex toys or covering them with a new condom each time. There is no vaccine against chlamydia.

Because many infections cause no symptoms, the NHS advises testing once a year or with a new sexual partner. A sexual health service can arrange testing, whether or not there are symptoms. The English programme also aims to reduce harm from untreated infection through faster results and treatment, partner notification and retesting. WHO has a global strategy that aims to reduce new chlamydia cases by 2030. Tests for other sexually transmitted infections are often recommended at the same time.

faqs.a: Yes. The NHS says chlamydia is curable with antibiotics. Partners are also tested and treated. The NHS says the risk of problems such as infertility is lower when the infection is treated early. People diagnosed are offered another test some months later to look for reinfection.

faqs.q: Can you have chlamydia without symptoms?
faqs.a: Yes. Most people with chlamydia do not notice any symptoms and may not know they have it. The CDC says it can still cause serious health problems, and can damage the reproductive system of a woman, even when there are no symptoms. This is why the NHS advises testing once a year or with a new sexual partner.

Untreated chlamydia can affect fertility. In women, pelvic inflammatory disease can lead to difficulty getting pregnant and a higher risk of ectopic pregnancy. The NHS says there is a possibility that untreated infection could affect fertility in men. The risk is lower if the infection is treated early.

faqs.q: How do tests for chlamydia work?
faqs.a: Testing uses a urine sample or a swab. The test most often used is a NAAT, which WHO describes as the gold standard. Some services offer online test kits. A sexual health service notes that a very recent infection may not show up straight away.

faqs.q: Is chlamydia spread by kissing or sharing towels?
faqs.a: No. The NHS says chlamydia is not spread by casual contact such as kissing, hugging or sharing towels or toilet seats. It is usually spread through vaginal, oral or anal sex, through contact with infected genital fluids, or by sharing sex toys that are not washed or covered with a new condom each time.

faqs.q: What does chlamydia mean for pregnancy?
faqs.a: An untreated infection can pass to the baby during birth. The baby may develop an eye infection or pneumonia. Untreated chlamydia in pregnancy may also increase the risk of premature labour and low birthweight. The CDC advises a pregnant person to talk to their healthcare provider about examination, testing and treatment.
